addedLines: Artifact: publishes pages on claude.ai; reads claude.ai artifact links. Load it with ToolSearch (select:Artifact) before writing any document, plan, analysis or visual, and whenever other people come up as readers, even after the work is written. Its description says whether to publish, offer a page or do neither. Once it is loaded, when the person wants something new made, Claude's first call is `action: "quickstart"` with the fitting `intent`, before loading a skill or writing a file. What follows applies whether or not it is loaded yet. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL. When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Culprit: Claude Code cloud prompts (team PiedPiper)

**Two repos:** `refunddesk` (the victim agent) and `piedpiper-neathacks` (Culprit, the product). `PRD.md` is already in the root of `piedpiper-neathacks`.

**Local setup:** everything runs locally on the MacBook. The two repos sit side by side:
- `.../Hackathons/neathack/piedpiper-neathacks` (Culprit)
- `.../Hackathons/neathack/refunddesk` (victim, create as its own git repo and GitHub repo)

Launch every session with `claude` from inside the repo folder it targets.

> **Note:** the parent folder `.../Hackathons/neathack/` has its own empty `.git` (no commits, no remote). Git inside each repo still uses that repo's own `.git`, but remove the outer one so nothing gets confused (`rm -rf .../Hackathons/neathack/.git`, your call).

**Why so many sessions:** Entire only captures sessions that start *after* `entire enable`. Each prompt below is one fresh `claude` session in one repo folder. The table numbers them in order.

**Before the first session:**
1. Put secrets in each repo's `.env` (gitignored). Load them with `set -a; source .env; set +a` before running `claude`.
2. Run `caffeinate -dims` in a spare terminal so the Mac doesn't sleep mid-run.
3. To steer from your phone, start `/remote-control` inside a session.

## Keeping the answers out of the victim repo

Entire records every refunddesk session, and Culprit reads those sessions to recover intent. So nothing in the refunddesk repo, its branch names, or its session transcripts may reveal which commit is the regression. Rules:

- **Neutral branch names:** `hist/a` … `hist/f`. No "scenario", "R1", "gap", "culprit", "regression" or "seed" anywhere in refunddesk code, commits or prompts.
- **The mapping lives only in this repo (Culprit), in this file and in `bench/`.** Never paste it into a refunddesk session.
- **You check out the branch yourself** (`git checkout hist/x`) *before* launching each culprit-change session, so the prompt never names a branch.
- **One session per culprit change**, containing only the realistic request.
- **Ground truth and strength checks run from the Culprit repo** (Prompt G), not from a refunddesk session.

### Scenario mapping (private, Culprit repo only)

| Branch | Scenario | Total commits | Culprit-change position | Uninstallable commit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `hist/a` | R3 (rename `order_id` → `id`) | 12 | #5 | — |
| `hist/b` | **R1 (hero, "make it faster")** | 14 | #10 | #7 (reverted by #8) |
| `hist/c` | R5 (shorter history window) | 13 | #9 | — |
| `hist/d` | R2 (prompt cleanup) | 15 | #6 | — |
| `hist/e` | R6 (lenient JSON parsing) | 12 | #8 | — |
| `hist/f` | R4 (`max_retries` → 0) | 16 | #12 | #8 (reverted by #9) |

Positions count from the first commit after `good-v1.0`. On `hist/b` the uninstallable commit sits at the midpoint, so the very first bisect step hits it, which shows the SKIP recovery in the hero demo.

## Run order (after Sat 12:30 IST)

| # | Session repo | Prompt | Can run in parallel with |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | refunddesk | A (bootstrap) | 2 |
| 2 | piedpiper-neathacks | A (bootstrap) | 1 |
| 3 | refunddesk | R part 1 (victim + eval suite + history up to the pause points) | 5 |
| 4 | refunddesk | R1 (hero session, after `git checkout hist/b`) | 5 |
| 5 | piedpiper-neathacks | C (build Culprit) | 3, 4, 6, 7 |
| 6 | refunddesk | S-a, S-c, S-d, S-e, S-f: five separate sessions, one per branch | 5 |
| 7 | refunddesk | Back in the R session: "Changes done. Continue the history." (R part 2) | 5 |
| 8 | piedpiper-neathacks | G (ground truth + strength check), when C isn't editing `bench/` | — |

---

## PROMPT A: Bootstrap (run in each repo, ~20 min, no product code)

1. **Install the Entire CLI** on this Mac, if it's missing, following https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/: `brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire`.
   - Run `entire enable --agent <claude-code integration name>` (confirm the name with `entire enable --help`).
   - Install graph: `entire plugin install graph`, then `entire graph init-agents --repo .`
   - Commit the `.entire/` files, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`.
2. **Install tooling if missing:**
   - `uv` (`brew install uv`)
   - the neatlogs CLI (`npm install --global neatlogs-cli@0.2.0`, needs Node 22+)

   Then set up readback with `neatlogs profile set work --host 'https://app.neatlogs.com'` and `neatlogs profile use work`. Run `neatlogs auth login --device` and wait for me to approve it in the browser. Add `.env` to `.gitignore`.
3. **Install the build-log skill.** Save https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/skill to `.claude/skills/neathack/SKILL.md`, then create `hackathon.md` with the sections it specifies.
4. **Check neatlogs:** `pip install neatlogs`, then `python -m neatlogs doctor --probe`. Report the results for TRACE_VISIBLE and TRACE_FINALIZED.
5. **Make one checkpointed commit.** Write a README stub, commit and push it, then show me the output of `entire checkpoint list`, `entire checkpoint explain HEAD` and `entire status`.
6. **Risk test (PRD §20).** Make a second small commit. Then run `entire checkpoint explain <full sha of the FIRST commit>`. Report whether an arbitrary SHA works and whether the output is parseable. Also report where Entire stores checkpoint data (branch or refs), and whether a fresh `git clone` of this repo can read it.

Report every failure with its exact error. Never fake output.

---

## PROMPT R: Build RefundDesk (victim) + history

> Paste into a refunddesk session. It deliberately contains no scenario details and no references to the Culprit repo or PRD.

## PROMPT G: Ground truth + strength check (piedpiper-neathacks, new session)

Run after R part 2 has finished and all `hist/*` branches are pushed.

1. Using the scenario mapping and culprit SHAs in `PROMPTS.md`, write `bench/scenarios.yaml` (branch, good ref `good-v1.0`, bad ref = branch head) and `bench/ground_truth.json` (culprit SHA, responsible hunk as file + line range, intended-gain metric). Work from `../refunddesk` read-only: use `git worktree add` under `.culprit/worktrees/` and never modify its checkout.
2. **R2 check:** confirm the >$500 escalation rule is missing from the system prompt at the `hist/d` culprit commit. If it's still there, stop and tell me.
3. **Uninstallable commits:** confirm `uv sync --locked` fails in a fresh worktree at `hist/b` #7 and `hist/f` #8, and succeeds at the commits right after them.
4. **Strength check (PRD §8.2):** run the full suite × 3 on `good-v1.0` and on each branch head, then compute Wilson 95% intervals. Start with `hist/b` (R1) and `hist/f` (R4), report cost per run, then do the rest. Report the table in `bench/strength.md`. Flag any regression whose interval overlaps the baseline; don't fix it here, tell me.
5. Never fabricate results.

---

## PROMPT C: Build Culprit (piedpiper-neathacks)

### Source of truth
`PRD.md` in this repo is the spec. Read all of it first; this prompt adds the execution rules. If the PRD and this prompt conflict, this prompt wins.

Commits must be dated during the hackathon. Follow `.claude/skills/neathack/SKILL.md` and update `hackathon.md` after every milestone with:
- one finding worth posting publicly
- one moment worth screenshotting

Never fabricate results. The PRD's honesty rules (§9.2, §14.1, §15) apply to every number.

### Rule zero: don't invent APIs
Before integrating, read these and record notes in `docs/research.md`:
- **neatlogs:** https://docs.neatlogs.com/llms.txt, the CLI, the Public API, the MCP tools reference, and the docs for Detections, Investigate/Fixes and prompt experiments.
- **Entire:** https://docs.entire.io, in particular `checkpoint explain` and where checkpoints are stored.
- **cfo.ai:** whether it imports from Google Sheets.

Any PRD feature the docs don't support goes to `BLOCKERS.md` with the fallback you chose. Never fake a tool's output.

### Models
Keep all model access in one module.
- `LLM_PROVIDER` is `anthropic` (default) or `openrouter` (OpenAI-compatible).
- `CULPRIT_MODEL` sets the model; never hardcode it.
- Validate structured outputs with pydantic. If validation fails, retry with a repair prompt, at most twice.

### The victim repo
- The victim repo is the sibling folder `../refunddesk`, configurable with `--repo`. It already has every branch, tag and Entire checkpoint ref locally.
- Culprit must only create worktrees from it, under `.culprit/worktrees/` (gitignored). It must never modify the checkout in `../refunddesk` itself.
- Install each worktree with `uv sync --locked`. An install failure means SKIP (PRD §8.1). Plain `uv sync` would silently re-resolve the broken pin, and `--frozen` would ignore it.
- Culprit drives RefundDesk through its eval runner. It sets `CULPRIT_RUN_ID`, `COMMIT_SHA`, `TASK_ID` and `REPETITION` so every victim trace is tagged.
- Until `hist/b` (R1) and `hist/f` (R4) exist upstream, build and test against a tiny throwaway fixture repo inside `tests/fixtures/`.

### Hour-1 risk gates (PRD §18)
1. **Entire:** `entire checkpoint explain <sha>` must work on a victim commit, run from `../refunddesk`. If it doesn't, implement the fallback (commit message plus diff, report states "intent unavailable") and log it.
2. **neatlogs:** read a victim trace back by trace ID through the CLI or Public API. If that fails, record tool logs locally and keep trace IDs as links only.

Report both results to me before building past the vertical slice.

### Intent leakage guard
- For `culprit bench`, the Localiser and Fixer must never see `bench/` ground truth, `PROMPTS.md`, or branch names. Pass only SHAs.
- Give the Localiser only the Entire context of the commit under examination, never that of neighbouring commits.
- Before any Entire text reaches an LLM, strip lines matching `hist/`, branch or ref names, `scenario`, `R[1-6]`, `culprit`, `regression`, `seed`, `gap`, `pause`. Log how many lines were removed, so the report can disclose it.

### neatlogs integration (mandatory, verbatim)
Run the task below as soon as the vertical slice runs end to end. Re-run its section 4 evidence loop after every milestone that adds or changes an LLM workflow: Planner, Task Selector, Localiser, Fixer, and the victim runs launched by Culprit.

Credentials:
- **Ingest:** `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`
- **Readback:** `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` if set; otherwise ask me to approve `neatlogs auth login --device`

Use the workflow labels `culprit` and `refunddesk`. Readback must prove that every Culprit stage, LLM call and non-LLM tool execution is a properly parented span in a finalized trace. Non-LLM tool executions include git and worktree operations, installs, eval runs, the Wilson decision, `entire` calls and verification. Every span must carry `run_id` and `commit_sha`.

```
# Integrate Neatlogs and verify every workflow

Integrate Neatlogs into the application in this working directory. Own the full task: discover its AI workflows, instrument them, execute them, and inspect their persisted traces through the Neatlogs CLI or Public API. Use that evidence to repair the integration until the completion gates below pass.

Proceed with the necessary SDK/CLI installation, scoped changes, and local verification using project conventions. Preserve unrelated work and application behavior. Ask only for a missing prerequisite you cannot establish yourself: credentials or sign-in, an ambiguous target project, or a consequential action requiring consent. Honor explicit repository approval requirements. Continue independent work while a prerequisite is pending.

## 1. Map coverage and load the matching guidance

Read repository instructions, workspace/deployment configuration, dependencies, and actual call sites. Follow shared client factories and wrappers to their callers. Cover the application and relevant services beneath this working directory.

Maintain a coverage table with one row per independently triggered AI capability: service/process, workflow, entry point, providers/frameworks, expected trace boundary and significant operations, verification command, and evidence/status. Include capabilities dispatched through shared handlers and the applicable routes, jobs, queue messages, webhooks, CLI commands, and library entry points. Account for discovered exclusions with a reason.

Start with [the docs index](https://docs.neatlogs.com/llms.txt) and [agent skills](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/skills). Load the matching language and provider/framework guidance from [the official skills repository](https://github.com/neatlogs/skills). Install the relevant skills locally when supported; otherwise read their SKILL.md files and triggered references directly. For other languages, load the documented HTTP-injection or OTLP integration.

**Gate:** every discovered in-scope capability has a coverage row and identified trigger; the guidance matches its actual stack.

## 2. Establish ingestion and authenticated readback

Set up both access paths:

| Process | Credential and context |
| --- | --- |
| Application exporting telemetry | Documented SDK ingest credential, usually `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`, and the selected ingest destination. |
| Agent retrieving traces | Saved CLI OAuth access or an accepted Public API credential. Prefer an expiring, project-bound service-account token via `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` for unattended verification. |

Reuse existing configuration and credentials. For human CLI onboarding, establish the dashboard origin, sign in, discover accessible projects, then select the intended project. Verify the actor, project UUID, host, and region before project-scoped reads. Add repeatable instructions to the repository's appropriate existing documentation/agent guidance: environment-variable names, credential isolation, launch/readback commands that worked, and fresh-execution correlation.

**Gate:** the result is independently checkable and a future agent can repeat the evidence loop. Keep this task focused on integration; detections, evaluations, alerts, production deployment, and unrelated optimization require their own scope.
```

### Milestones
These follow PRD §18. Commit and push at each one.

1. **M1: vertical slice.**
   - Work: ledger, simple bisect (no resampling), worktree sandbox with `uv sync --locked`, eval runner, and `culprit run` finding R1 (`hist/b`) end to end against the victim. Then the neatlogs integration task, until it reports PASS.
   - Exit: R1 found, with the run traced.
2. **M2: noise and recovery.**
   - Work: the Wilson rule (§8.2), resampling, skip semantics, budget caps, `culprit resume`.
   - Exit: all six branches run, and a recorded run shows ≥1 SKIP and ≥1 INCONCLUSIVE→resample.
3. **M3: benchmark v1.**
   - Work: `culprit bench`, reading `bench/scenarios.yaml` (from Prompt G). Freeze the code, then run `bench --tag v1`.
   - Exit: actual v1 numbers recorded in `evidence/bench-v1.md`, with trace links.
4. **M4: improve using neatlogs.**
   - Work: use whichever of Investigate/Fixes, Detections and prompt experiments really exist to diagnose v1's misses. Fix Culprit in a dedicated session, so its Entire checkpoint becomes the headline evidence. Then run `bench --tag v2`.
   - Exit: `evidence/IMPROVEMENT.md` with the v1 vs v2 table, what the traces revealed, and the checkpoint link and ID.
5. **M5: localise, fix, verify.**
   - Work: §8.3, §8.4 and §10, including held-out tasks and the fallback to a single-hunk revert.
   - Exit: the R1 fix verified, keeping the parallel calls and restoring validation, with quality and latency in a table.
6. **M6: report and costs.**
   - Work: markdown and HTML reports (§13), plus `culprit export-costs`.
   - Exit: generate `business/cfo-inputs.md` from the measured ledger costs, with pricing scenarios A, B and C as hypotheses and a placeholder for the cfo.ai export, which I'll make by hand.
7. **M7: docs.**
   - Work: README (problem, setup, run, the role of each tool, the honesty note on seeded regressions, limitations), `DEMO.md` following PRD §17, and `evidence/SUMMARY.md` linking every claim to a trace, checkpoint, commit or file. Run the neatlogs evidence loop one last time.
   - Exit: a clean run from a fresh clone.

**Stretch work (PRD §6) starts only after M7.** Follow the PRD's cut order if time runs short. Never cut what the PRD lists under "never cut".

### Quality bar
- **Tests:** unit tests for the Wilson decision, the bisect controller with skip semantics, idempotent ledger writes and resume, the verifier gates, and the intent-leakage filter.
- **Configuration:** deterministic everything except the LLM calls. Config constants are recorded in the ledger for every run.
- **Code:** small typed modules, no dead code.
- **Asking:** ask only when truly blocked. Otherwise decide, log it in `hackathon.md`, and continue.

published requirements with the builder. Never register, publish, deploy or submit
on their behalf without their instruction. This skill does not establish contest
rules and does not automatically qualify a project.

# Culprit — Product Requirements Document

**Team:** PiedPiper · **Event:** neatHack 2026 (Oct 10–12, IST) · **Status:** Final for build · **Version:** 1.0 (Oct 10, pre-kickoff)

> One line: **`git bisect` for agent behaviour, with receipts.** Give Culprit a good ref, a bad ref and an eval suite. It finds the commit that broke your agent, explains *why* that change was made (from the Entire session), writes the smallest fix that restores quality while keeping the intended gain, and proves it statistically.

---

## 1. Problem

Teams shipping LLM agents change prompts, swap models, tweak tools and merge coding-agent commits many times a week. Quality degrades silently. When the eval pass rate drops from 90% to 60% across 15 commits:

- Re-running evals by hand at each commit takes hours to a day.
- LLM evals are noisy, so a single run per commit gives misleading answers. Classic `git bisect` assumes a deterministic test.
- Even after finding the commit, nobody remembers *why* it was made. Reverting it throws away the intended improvement (e.g. a latency win).

**Why now:** Coding agents write a growing share of agent code. Entire captures the session intent behind each commit, and neatlogs captures the traces of every agent run. Culprit is the first workflow that joins **intent (Entire) + behaviour (neatlogs) + statistics** to answer "what broke, why, and how do we fix it without losing the gain?"

## 2. Users and buyer

| Persona | Situation | What they want |
|---|---|---|
| **Agent engineer** (primary user) | Pass rate dropped after a week of changes | The culprit commit and a verified fix in minutes, not a day |
| **Eng lead / AI platform owner** (buyer) | Regressions reach production; nobody owns eval hygiene | A regression gate + root-cause report attached to every PR |
| **Coding-agent-heavy teams** | Many commits come from agent sessions with thin commit messages | The "why" behind each change, recovered from session context |

## 3. Goals and non-goals

### Goals (hackathon)
1. **G1** — Correctly identify the culprit commit on a seeded-regression benchmark with known ground truth.
2. **G2** — Make noisy evals usable: statistical decision rule, resampling, explicit "inconclusive" state.
3. **G3** — Recover from real failures: uninstallable commits, flaky tools, killed process, budget exhaustion.
4. **G4** — Localise to the responsible hunk and produce a minimal fix that restores quality and preserves the intended gain, verified on held-out tasks.
5. **G5** — Deep, natural use of neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai, with a measured v1 → v2 improvement of Culprit itself.

- Not a general eval framework (we consume a simple suite format).
- No hosted multi-tenant SaaS, auth or billing during the hackathon.
- No support for arbitrary languages/frameworks: Python victim agents only.
- No automatic PR merging. Culprit proposes; humans merge.

## 4. Hackathon fit

| Rubric item (weight) | How Culprit scores |
|---|---|
| **The agent (30%)** | Plans a search, uses tools (git, worktrees, eval runner, neatlogs readback, Entire CLI), keeps state (SQLite ledger), recovers (skip/resample/resume/budget), verifies (CI-based decision + held-out suite) |
| **Required tools (25%)** | neatlogs and Entire are *inputs to the product*, not decoration; cfo.ai is fed measured cost-per-bisect from the ledger |
| **Demo (20%)** | "Make it faster" → validation removed → Culprit finds it, keeps the speedup, restores quality |
| **Building in public (15%)** | Honest v1 failures, recovery clip, before/after card (§16) |
| **Usefulness/originality (10%)** | Real, recurring pain for the exact audience of neatlogs/Entire |

**Mandatory submission items** (from neatlogs.com/hackathon): demo video ≤ 3 min covering all three tools · cfo.ai business plan · before/after run with compared numbers · neatlogs traces/screenshots · Entire checkpoints (link + ID) · a run showing recovery from a failed action · public share links tagged #neatHack · public repo with commits dated during the hackathon · X quote-post of the official neatlogs post with team name, project name, repo and demo.

## 5. User stories (MVP)

1. *As an agent engineer*, I run `culprit run --good v1.0 --bad HEAD --suite evals/` and get the culprit commit with a confidence statement.
2. *As an agent engineer*, I see each tested commit's pass rate with a 95% Wilson interval, cost and latency, plus links to the neatlogs traces of the failing runs.
3. *As an agent engineer*, I read *why* the culprit commit was made (the Entire session prompt/summary) next to the diff.
4. *As an agent engineer*, I get a minimal patch (one or more hunks) that restores quality, with evidence that the intended gain (e.g. latency) is retained.
5. *As an agent engineer*, if Culprit is killed mid-run, `culprit resume <run_id>` continues without re-running completed work.

# neatHack 2026 build log: Culprit

## Project

- **Name:** Culprit
- **Purpose:** `git bisect` for agent behaviour, with receipts. Given a good ref, a bad ref and an eval suite, Culprit finds the commit that broke an LLM agent, explains why that change was made (from its Entire session), writes the smallest fix that restores quality while keeping the intended gain, and proves it statistically.
- **Problem:** LLM agent quality degrades silently across many commits. Evals are noisy, so classic `git bisect` gives misleading answers, and nobody remembers why a breaking change was made. Reverting it also throws away the intended gain.

## Team

- Team PiedPiper. Member names/handles: *pending, the builder will choose what to publish.*

## Stack

Planned (from `PRD.md`); move items to "used" as they are integrated.

- **Used so far:** Entire CLI 0.11.4 (checkpoints on git refs), neatlogs CLI 0.2.0, `uv`, Claude Code.
- **Planned:** Python + `uv`, SQLite ledger, neatlogs Python SDK for tracing, Anthropic or OpenRouter for LLM calls, cfo.ai for the business plan. The victim agent is `refunddesk`, a separate repo.

## Build log

### 2026-10-10

- **Done:** Bootstrap (Prompt A). Entire is enabled with `git-refs` checkpoints, and the neathack build-log skill is installed at `.claude/skills/neathack/SKILL.md`. Results from the README commit and the `checkpoint explain` risk test are recorded below once they've been run.
- **Planned:** Prompt C, starting with M1 (vertical slice) and the hour-1 risk gates (Entire `checkpoint explain` on a victim commit, plus neatlogs trace readback).

## Demo

- *Pending.* No demo URL yet.

## Known limitations and next steps

- Culprit hasn't been built yet. Next: M1 vertical slice per `PROMPTS.md` (Prompt C).

## Submission

Requirements confirmed from https://neatlogs.com/hackathon (read 2026-10-10):

- [ ] Uses neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai (cfo.ai business plan covering pricing, costs, revenue, runway)
- [ ] Before/after run of the agent with compared numbers (e.g., two neatlogs traces)
- [ ] neatlogs trace links or screenshots
- [ ] Entire checkpoints or entire-graph output
- [ ] A run where an action failed, showing what the agent did next
- [ ] Building-in-public links tagged #neatHack
- [ ] Public repo with commits dated during the hackathon
- [ ] Demo video (the length limit isn't on the page; the PRD says ≤ 3 min, *pending confirmation*)
- [ ] Submit on X by quoting the official neatlogs post with team, name, project, public repo and demo. Window: Mon 12 Oct 2026, 7:00–11:55 PM IST

Judging weights (published): agent 30%, use of neatlogs/Entire/cfo.ai 25%, demo video 20%, building in public 15%, usefulness/originality 10%.

content.content:
60	5. *As an agent engineer*, if Culprit is killed mid-run, `culprit resume <run_id>` continues without re-running completed work.
61	6. *As a lead*, I get a shareable HTML report I can attach to a PR.
62	
63	## 6. Scope
64	
65	### MVP (must ship)
66	- `culprit` CLI: `run`, `resume`, `report`, `bench`.
67	- Victim agent + 20-task eval suite with deterministic checkers.
68	- Victim repo history with **6 seeded regressions** and noise commits, including one uninstallable commit.
69	- Noise-aware bisect: Wilson interval decision rule, resampling, skip semantics, budget caps.
70	- SQLite run ledger; resumable.
71	- neatlogs tracing of every victim run and of Culprit's own reasoning; trace links in the report.
72	- Entire checkpoint context for the culprit commit (with a documented fallback).
73	- Hunk localisation + fix + verification on full suite + held-out tasks.
74	- Markdown and static HTML report.
75	- Benchmark harness (`culprit bench`) scoring Culprit against ground truth, used for the v1 → v2 comparison.
76	- Cost export (CSV/Google Sheet) for cfo.ai.
77	
78	### Stretch (only after MVP is frozen)
79	- GitHub Action: run Culprit on a PR when the eval pass rate drops.
80	- Entire Trail for the v1 → v2 fix of Culprit (requires Trails access from the Entire team).
81	- Entire Graph used by our coding agent during the build.
82	- Multi-culprit detection (two independent regressions in one range).
83	- Small web viewer for reports.
84	
85	### Cut order (drop first → last)
86	1. Web viewer → 2. GitHub Action → 3. Multi-culprit → 4. HTML report (keep markdown) → 5. Held-out tasks (keep full-suite verification) → 6. Automatic fix writing (fall back to "revert hunk X" + re-verification).
87	
88	**Never cut:** seeded benchmark with ground truth, ledger, decision rule, recovery paths, neatlogs traces, Entire checkpoints, cfo.ai plan.
89	
90	## 7. System design
91	
92	```
93	                ┌──────────────────────────── Culprit (orchestrator agent) ───────────────────────────┐
94	 culprit run ──▶│ Planner ─▶ Bisect Controller ─▶ Commit Evaluator ─▶ Decision Rule ─▶ Localiser ─▶ Fixer │
95	                │     │              │                   │                               │           │
96	                │     ▼              ▼                   ▼                               ▼           │
97	                │  Task Selector   Worktree Sandbox    Eval Runner ──▶ Victim Agent    Verifier      │
98	                │     ▲                                   │  (mock tools)                │           │
99	                │     └── neatlogs readback ◀─────────────┘                              ▼           │
100	                │                                                     Entire context   Report        │
101	                └───────────────────────────────── SQLite Run Ledger ─────────────────────────────────┘
102	```
103	
104	| Component | Type | Responsibility |
105	|---|---|---|
106	| **Planner** | LLM | Reads suite + good/bad baselines, sets sampling plan (k, task subset) within budget |
107	| **Task Selector** | Deterministic + LLM | Deterministically ranks tasks by pass-rate delta (good vs bad); LLM inspects failing traces to choose a small *discriminating* subset and avoid flaky tasks |
108	| **Bisect Controller** | Deterministic | Midpoint selection over `git rev-list --first-parent good..bad`, skip semantics, state transitions |
109	| **Worktree Sandbox** | Deterministic | `git worktree add` per commit, isolated venv install (`uv`), timeouts, cleanup |
110	| **Eval Runner** | Deterministic | Runs victim agent on tasks × k, applies checkers, records pass/fail, cost, latency, trace ID |
111	| **Decision Rule** | Deterministic | Wilson 95% interval vs threshold → GOOD / BAD / INCONCLUSIVE (§8.2) |
112	| **Localiser** | LLM + deterministic check | Ranks culprit hunks using diff + Entire intent + failing traces; tests single-hunk reverts |
113	| **Fixer** | LLM | Writes a minimal patch that restores behaviour while keeping the intent (e.g. keep caching, restore validation) |
114	| **Verifier** | Deterministic | Full suite + held-out tasks × k on `bad+fix`; checks quality CI and intended-gain metric (§10) |
115	| **Ledger** | SQLite | Every step, result, cost; enables resume and cfo.ai export |
116	| **Report** | Deterministic | Markdown/HTML with timeline, CIs, diff, intent, trace links, checkpoint links, costs |
117	
118	### Stack
119	Python 3.12 · `uv` · Typer (CLI) · SQLite (`sqlite3`) · Anthropic SDK (Claude) · neatlogs Python SDK + CLI/Public API · Entire CLI · Jinja2 (report) · pytest.
120	Models: a cheap, fast model for the victim agent (temperature 0) and a stronger model for Culprit's reasoning steps. Exact model IDs chosen at kickoff from current pricing.
121	
122	## 8. Core algorithms
123	
124	### 8.1 Noise-aware bisect
125	1. Evaluate `good` and `bad` refs on the full suite × k. Abort with a clear message if the gap isn't significant (CIs overlap) — "no regression to bisect".
126	2. Threshold `t = (p_good + p_bad) / 2`.
127	3. Task Selector picks the discriminating subset `D` (default 8 tasks) from tasks that pass on good and fail on bad.
128	4. Loop over the candidate range (first-parent history):
129	   - Pick midpoint `m`. Create worktree, install.
130	   - **Install/import fails** → mark `SKIP`, test the nearest untested neighbour (alternate left/right), like `git bisect skip`.
131	   - Run `D × k` (default k=3). Apply decision rule.
132	   - **INCONCLUSIVE** → resample (add k more runs, then widen to more tasks) up to a per-commit cap. If still inconclusive, decide by point estimate and flag the step `low_confidence`.
133	5. Output: first BAD commit after the last GOOD commit. If a SKIP commit sits on the boundary, report the range (as `git bisect` does).
134	
135	### 8.2 Decision rule (deterministic)
136	For a commit with `s` passes in `n` runs, compute the 95% Wilson score interval `[L, U]`.
137	- `L ≥ t` → **GOOD**
138	- `U ≤ t` → **BAD**
139	- otherwise → **INCONCLUSIVE**
140	
141	Constants (`z = 1.96`, k, caps) live in config and are recorded in the ledger for every run.
142	
143	### 8.3 Localisation
144	1. Split the culprit diff into hunks.
145	2. LLM ranks hunks using: the diff, the Entire session intent for that commit, and the failing traces (tool calls, errors) pulled from neatlogs.
146	3. For the top-N hunks (default 3), apply the reverse of that single hunk on `bad` and run `D × k`. The first hunk whose revert flips BAD → GOOD is the responsible hunk. If none do, try pairs (cap), then fall back to "whole commit".
147	
148	### 8.4 Fix
149	The Fixer gets: the responsible hunk, the commit intent (e.g. "make it faster"), and the intended-gain metric. It writes a patch that restores the lost behaviour **without** reverting the whole commit (e.g. keep the parallel tool calls, restore result validation). If its patch fails verification twice, fall back to the single-hunk revert, which is already verified.
150	
151	## 9. Victim agent and seeded benchmark
152	
153	### 9.1 Victim agent: "RefundDesk"
154	A customer-support agent that resolves refund requests using **mock tools** backed by a local JSON store:
155	`lookup_order`, `get_refund_policy`, `issue_refund`, `escalate_to_human`, `send_customer_email`.
156	The mock layer can inject failures (timeouts, `status: failed` payloads) deterministically per task seed.
157	
158	**Eval suite:** 20 tasks + 6 held-out tasks. Each task = customer message + initial store state + **deterministic checker** on the final store state and tool-call log (e.g. "refund issued exactly once for ≤ $500", "escalated when order not found", "no refund when lookup failed").
159	
160	### 9.2 Seeded regressions (ground truth)
161	Each scenario is a commit range of ~12–16 commits in the separate victim repo, with noise commits (docs, refactors, logging) around one culprit.
162	
163	| ID | Culprit change | Intended gain | Symptom |
164	|---|---|---|---|
165	| **R1 (hero)** | "Make it faster": coding agent parallelises tool calls and **removes tool-result validation** | Lower latency | Refunds issued when `lookup_order` failed |
166	| R2 | Prompt cleanup drops the "> $500 needs escalation" rule | Shorter prompt / cost | Large refunds issued without escalation |
167	| R3 | Tool schema renames `order_id` → `id` without updating the description | API consistency | Wrong/missing arguments on lookup |
168	| R4 | `max_retries` 3 → 0 "to reduce latency" | Latency | Fails on flaky-tool tasks |
169	| R5 | Conversation history window shortened | Token cost | Loses customer details from earlier turns |
170	| R6 | Lenient JSON parsing of tool calls | Fewer parse errors | Malformed calls executed with defaults |
171	
172	Plus **one uninstallable commit** (broken dependency pin) placed near the midpoint of at least two scenarios, to exercise skip recovery.
173	
174	**Honesty rule:** The regressions are deliberately seeded. R1 is created through a real coding-agent session (captured by Entire) given the instruction "make it faster". We say this plainly in the demo and README.
175	
176	## 10. Verification
177	
178	A fix is **verified** only if all hold:
179	1. **Quality:** On full suite + held-out tasks × k, the Wilson interval for `bad+fix` overlaps or exceeds the `good` baseline interval.
180	2. **Intended gain kept:** The intent metric (latency / tokens / cost, taken from the commit intent) for `bad+fix` is no worse than `bad` by more than a configured tolerance.
181	3. **No new failures:** No task that passes on `good` fails consistently (all k) on `bad+fix`.
182	
183	**Benchmark verification of Culprit itself** (`culprit bench`): for each of R1–R6, record whether the culprit commit was correct, whether the hunk was correct, whether the fix verified, victim runs used, cost, wall time. Ground truth is stored in `bench/ground_truth.json` in the Culprit repo (never in the victim repo). Victim history branches use neutral names (`hist/a`…`hist/f`); the scenario mapping lives only in the Culprit repo.
184	
185	## 11. Failure handling and recovery
186	
187	| Failure | Detection | Recovery | Shown in demo? |
188	|---|---|---|---|
189	| Commit won't install/import | Non-zero exit / import error in worktree | Mark SKIP, test neighbours | **Yes** |
190	| Noisy result (e.g. 3/5) | Wilson interval straddles threshold | Resample up to cap; flag `low_confidence` | **Yes** |
191	| Process killed | Ledger has incomplete run | `culprit resume <run_id>` skips completed steps | Yes (short) |
192	| LLM/API rate limit or 5xx | Exception from SDK | Exponential backoff, then mark step retryable | Trace only |
193	| Budget cap hit | Ledger cost ≥ cap | Stop, report best current range + what remains | Trace only |
194	| Fixer patch fails verification | Verifier fails | Retry once with failure evidence, then fall back to verified hunk revert | If it happens |
195	| Entire context unavailable | CLI error / empty output | Use commit message + diff; report states "intent unavailable" | No |
196	| No significant regression | good/bad CIs overlap | Exit cleanly with explanation | No |
197	
198	## 12. Data model (SQLite ledger)
199	
200	- `runs(run_id, repo, good_ref, bad_ref, suite_hash, config_json, status, started_at, finished_at, total_cost_usd, culprit_sha, confidence)`
201	- `steps(step_id, run_id, kind[baseline|bisect|resample|localise|fix|verify], commit_sha, status, decision, wilson_low, wilson_high, n, passes, cost_usd, latency_ms_p50, started_at, finished_at, error)`
202	- `task_runs(id, step_id, task_id, repetition, passed, cost_usd, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, neatlogs_trace_id)`
203	- `llm_calls(id, run_id, step_id, purpose, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_usd, neatlogs_trace_id)`
204	- `artifacts(id, run_id, kind[intent|diff|patch|report], path_or_text)`
205	
206	Every write is idempotent by `(run_id, step kind, commit_sha, task_id, repetition)` so resume never double-counts.
207	
208	## 13. CLI
209	
210	```bash
211	culprit run --repo ../refunddesk --good <ref> --bad <ref> --suite evals/ \
212	            [--k 3] [--budget-usd 3.00] [--heldout evals/heldout/] [--no-fix]
213	culprit resume <run_id>
214	culprit report <run_id> [--html out/report.html]
215	culprit bench --scenarios bench/scenarios.yaml [--tag v1|v2]
216	culprit export-costs [--format csv] > costs.csv     # input for cfo.ai
217	```
218	
219	**Report contents:** verdict + confidence · bisect timeline (commit, decision, Wilson interval, n, cost, latency) · skipped commits · culprit diff with responsible hunk highlighted · Entire intent + checkpoint link/ID · links to failing neatlogs traces · proposed patch · verification table (good / bad / bad+fix: quality CI, latency, cost) · total cost and victim runs.
220	
221	## 14. Required tools
222	
223	### 14.1 neatlogs
224	- **Tracing:** every victim task run is a trace tagged `commit_sha`, `task_id`, `repetition`, `run_id`. Culprit's own LLM calls are traced separately.
225	- **Readback:** Task Selector and Localiser pull failing traces via the neatlogs CLI/Public API.
226	- **Detections:** regex rule on tool results containing `"status": "failed"` followed by `issue_refund`; condition rules such as `cost_usd > <cap>` for runaway runs.
227	- **Investigate:** used on Culprit **v1** benchmark runs to find why it misidentified or wasted runs.
228	- **Experiments (prompt versions):** Culprit's Localiser/Task Selector prompts versioned; v1 → v2 promoted by label.
229	- **Before/after:** `culprit bench --tag v1` and `--tag v2` on the same 6 scenarios. Metrics: culprit accuracy (x/6), hunk accuracy, fix verified (x/6), victim runs per bisect, cost per bisect, wall time. **Numbers are whatever the runs produce; nothing is estimated or rounded in our favour.**
230	
231	**Instrumentation plan (apply at 12:30, from docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python):**
232	- Install `pip install -U "neatlogs[anthropic]"` (Python ≥ 3.10, < 3.14). Key from `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` in `.env` (gitignored), never hardcoded. Default endpoint `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`.
233	- Two workflow names, one per entry point: `culprit-bisect` (Culprit CLI `run`/`resume`/`bench`) and `refunddesk-support-agent` (each victim task run, launched as a subprocess in a worktree).
234	- Capture Anthropic calls with **one** mechanism only: `neatlogs.wrap(Anthropic())` (the docs example uses OpenAI; Anthropic auto-detection is stated, not shown), or `instrumentations=["anthropic"]` with `init()` before the import. Never both.
235	- `@neatlogs.span(kind="WORKFLOW")` on each CLI command and on the victim's task entry point; `kind="TOOL"` on mock tools and on Culprit's git/worktree/eval tools; `kind="AGENT"` on Selector/Localiser/Fixer.
236	- Per-run metadata via `wrap()` kwargs (`commit_sha`, `task_id`, `repetition`, `run_id`), which become `neatlogs.workflow.<key>`. This is inferred from the docs, so verify in the dashboard.
237	- Both entry points are one-shot processes, so call `neatlogs.flush()` then `neatlogs.shutdown()` at exit (in `finally`).
238	- Open: the docs don't show how to read the current trace ID. Ask on Discord or use the CLI/Public API to look traces up by `run_id`/`task_id` metadata.
239	
240	### 14.2 Entire
241	- Both repos (`piedpiper-neathacks` = Culprit, `refunddesk` = victim) connected via the Entire GitHub App; `entire enable` in each.
242	- **Product use:** Culprit reads the culprit commit's session context (`entire checkpoint explain <sha>`) to recover intent.
243	- **Build use:** every meaningful commit of Culprit is checkpointed; the checkpoint for the v1 → v2 fix is the headline evidence (Sessions → Changes).
244	- **Trails** (if access granted): the v1 → v2 fix done as a Trail. **Graph** optional.
245	- Submission includes checkpoint link `https://entire.io/gh/OWNER/REPO/commit/FULL_SHA` and checkpoint ID.
246	
247	### 14.3 cfo.ai
248	- **Input:** `culprit export-costs` → Google Sheet (cfo.ai lists Google Sheets as a data connection; fall back to manual upload/entry if the import doesn't work).
249	- **Measured actuals:** cost per victim run, victim runs per bisect, Culprit LLM cost per bisect, wall time.
250	- **Pricing scenarios to model** (hypotheses, not facts):
251	  - **A. Flat SaaS:** $49 / $199 per repo/month with a bisect quota.
252	  - **B. Customer's own model key + platform fee** (recommended hypothesis): customer pays victim-run LLM cost; we charge a platform fee.
253	  - **C. Metered:** platform fee + per-bisect charge.
254	- **Questions for Ari:** gross margin per customer under A vs B at 10/50/200 bisects/month · break-even repos with 2 founders · runway under base/upside/downside acquisition · stress test with a 10× more expensive victim agent.
255	- **Deliverable:** exported business plan (pricing, costs, revenue, runway) in `/business/` and linked from the README.
256	
257	## 15. Success metrics
258	
259	| Metric | Target for submission |
260	|---|---|
261	| Culprit accuracy on R1–R6 | Reported for v1 and v2 (aim: v2 ≥ v1 and ≥ 5/6) |
262	| Fix verified on R1 | Required for the demo |
263	| Recovery shown | ≥ 1 skip and ≥ 1 resample in a recorded run |
264	| Cost per bisect | Measured and within the per-bisect budget cap |
265	| Evidence complete | All mandatory submission items in §4 present |
266	
267	Targets are aims, not claims. The README reports actual values only.
268

5. *As an agent engineer*, if Culprit is killed mid-run, `culprit resume <run_id>` continues without re-running completed work.
6. *As a lead*, I get a shareable HTML report I can attach to a PR.

## 6. Scope

### MVP (must ship)
- `culprit` CLI: `run`, `resume`, `report`, `bench`.
- Victim agent + 20-task eval suite with deterministic checkers.
- Victim repo history with **6 seeded regressions** and noise commits, including one uninstallable commit.
- Noise-aware bisect: Wilson interval decision rule, resampling, skip semantics, budget caps.
- SQLite run ledger; resumable.
- neatlogs tracing of every victim run and of Culprit's own reasoning; trace links in the report.
- Entire checkpoint context for the culprit commit (with a documented fallback).
- Hunk localisation + fix + verification on full suite + held-out tasks.
- Markdown and static HTML report.
- Benchmark harness (`culprit bench`) scoring Culprit against ground truth, used for the v1 → v2 comparison.
- Cost export (CSV/Google Sheet) for cfo.ai.

### Stretch (only after MVP is frozen)
- GitHub Action: run Culprit on a PR when the eval pass rate drops.
- Entire Trail for the v1 → v2 fix of Culprit (requires Trails access from the Entire team).
- Entire Graph used by our coding agent during the build.
- Multi-culprit detection (two independent regressions in one range).
- Small web viewer for reports.

### Cut order (drop first → last)
1. Web viewer → 2. GitHub Action → 3. Multi-culprit → 4. HTML report (keep markdown) → 5. Held-out tasks (keep full-suite verification) → 6. Automatic fix writing (fall back to "revert hunk X" + re-verification).

**Never cut:** seeded benchmark with ground truth, ledger, decision rule, recovery paths, neatlogs traces, Entire checkpoints, cfo.ai plan.

## 7. System design

```
                ┌──────────────────────────── Culprit (orchestrator agent) ───────────────────────────┐
 culprit run ──▶│ Planner ─▶ Bisect Controller ─▶ Commit Evaluator ─▶ Decision Rule ─▶ Localiser ─▶ Fixer │
                │     │              │                   │                               │           │
                │     ▼              ▼                   ▼                               ▼           │
                │  Task Selector   Worktree Sandbox    Eval Runner ──▶ Victim Agent    Verifier      │
                │     ▲                                   │  (mock tools)                │           │
                │     └── neatlogs readback ◀─────────────┘                              ▼           │
                │                                                     Entire context   Report        │
                └───────────────────────────────── SQLite Run Ledger ─────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Component | Type | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| **Planner** | LLM | Reads suite + good/bad baselines, sets sampling plan (k, task subset) within budget |
| **Task Selector** | Deterministic + LLM | Deterministically ranks tasks by pass-rate delta (good vs bad); LLM inspects failing traces to choose a small *discriminating* subset and avoid flaky tasks |
| **Bisect Controller** | Deterministic | Midpoint selection over `git rev-list --first-parent good..bad`, skip semantics, state transitions |
| **Worktree Sandbox** | Deterministic | `git worktree add` per commit, isolated venv install (`uv`), timeouts, cleanup |
| **Eval Runner** | Deterministic | Runs victim agent on tasks × k, applies checkers, records pass/fail, cost, latency, trace ID |
| **Decision Rule** | Deterministic | Wilson 95% interval vs threshold → GOOD / BAD / INCONCLUSIVE (§8.2) |
| **Localiser** | LLM + deterministic check | Ranks culprit hunks using diff + Entire intent + failing traces; tests single-hunk reverts |
| **Fixer** | LLM | Writes a minimal patch that restores behaviour while keeping the intent (e.g. keep caching, restore validation) |
| **Verifier** | Deterministic | Full suite + held-out tasks × k on `bad+fix`; checks quality CI and intended-gain metric (§10) |
| **Ledger** | SQLite | Every step, result, cost; enables resume and cfo.ai export |
| **Report** | Deterministic | Markdown/HTML with timeline, CIs, diff, intent, trace links, checkpoint links, costs |

### Stack
Python 3.12 · `uv` · Typer (CLI) · SQLite (`sqlite3`) · Anthropic SDK (Claude) · neatlogs Python SDK + CLI/Public API · Entire CLI · Jinja2 (report) · pytest.
Models: a cheap, fast model for the victim agent (temperature 0) and a stronger model for Culprit's reasoning steps. Exact model IDs chosen at kickoff from current pricing.

## 8. Core algorithms

### 8.1 Noise-aware bisect
1. Evaluate `good` and `bad` refs on the full suite × k. Abort with a clear message if the gap isn't significant (CIs overlap) — "no regression to bisect".
2. Threshold `t = (p_good + p_bad) / 2`.
3. Task Selector picks the discriminating subset `D` (default 8 tasks) from tasks that pass on good and fail on bad.
4. Loop over the candidate range (first-parent history):
   - Pick midpoint `m`. Create worktree, install.
   - **Install/import fails** → mark `SKIP`, test the nearest untested neighbour (alternate left/right), like `git bisect skip`.
   - Run `D × k` (default k=3). Apply decision rule.
   - **INCONCLUSIVE** → resample (add k more runs, then widen to more tasks) up to a per-commit cap. If still inconclusive, decide by point estimate and flag the step `low_confidence`.
5. Output: first BAD commit after the last GOOD commit. If a SKIP commit sits on the boundary, report the range (as `git bisect` does).

### 8.2 Decision rule (deterministic)
For a commit with `s` passes in `n` runs, compute the 95% Wilson score interval `[L, U]`.
- `L ≥ t` → **GOOD**
- `U ≤ t` → **BAD**
- otherwise → **INCONCLUSIVE**

Constants (`z = 1.96`, k, caps) live in config and are recorded in the ledger for every run.

### 8.3 Localisation
1. Split the culprit diff into hunks.
2. LLM ranks hunks using: the diff, the Entire session intent for that commit, and the failing traces (tool calls, errors) pulled from neatlogs.
3. For the top-N hunks (default 3), apply the reverse of that single hunk on `bad` and run `D × k`. The first hunk whose revert flips BAD → GOOD is the responsible hunk. If none do, try pairs (cap), then fall back to "whole commit".

### 8.4 Fix
The Fixer gets: the responsible hunk, the commit intent (e.g. "make it faster"), and the intended-gain metric. It writes a patch that restores the lost behaviour **without** reverting the whole commit (e.g. keep the parallel tool calls, restore result validation). If its patch fails verification twice, fall back to the single-hunk revert, which is already verified.

## 9. Victim agent and seeded benchmark

### 9.1 Victim agent: "RefundDesk"
A customer-support agent that resolves refund requests using **mock tools** backed by a local JSON store:
`lookup_order`, `get_refund_policy`, `issue_refund`, `escalate_to_human`, `send_customer_email`.
The mock layer can inject failures (timeouts, `status: failed` payloads) deterministically per task seed.

**Eval suite:** 20 tasks + 6 held-out tasks. Each task = customer message + initial store state + **deterministic checker** on the final store state and tool-call log (e.g. "refund issued exactly once for ≤ $500", "escalated when order not found", "no refund when lookup failed").

### 9.2 Seeded regressions (ground truth)
Each scenario is a commit range of ~12–16 commits in the separate victim repo, with noise commits (docs, refactors, logging) around one culprit.

| ID | Culprit change | Intended gain | Symptom |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R1 (hero)** | "Make it faster": coding agent parallelises tool calls and **removes tool-result validation** | Lower latency | Refunds issued when `lookup_order` failed |
| R2 | Prompt cleanup drops the "> $500 needs escalation" rule | Shorter prompt / cost | Large refunds issued without escalation |
| R3 | Tool schema renames `order_id` → `id` without updating the description | API consistency | Wrong/missing arguments on lookup |
| R4 | `max_retries` 3 → 0 "to reduce latency" | Latency | Fails on flaky-tool tasks |
| R5 | Conversation history window shortened | Token cost | Loses customer details from earlier turns |
| R6 | Lenient JSON parsing of tool calls | Fewer parse errors | Malformed calls executed with defaults |

Plus **one uninstallable commit** (broken dependency pin) placed near the midpoint of at least two scenarios, to exercise skip recovery.

**Honesty rule:** The regressions are deliberately seeded. R1 is created through a real coding-agent session (captured by Entire) given the instruction "make it faster". We say this plainly in the demo and README.

## 10. Verification

A fix is **verified** only if all hold:
1. **Quality:** On full suite + held-out tasks × k, the Wilson interval for `bad+fix` overlaps or exceeds the `good` baseline interval.
2. **Intended gain kept:** The intent metric (latency / tokens / cost, taken from the commit intent) for `bad+fix` is no worse than `bad` by more than a configured tolerance.
3. **No new failures:** No task that passes on `good` fails consistently (all k) on `bad+fix`.

**Benchmark verification of Culprit itself** (`culprit bench`): for each of R1–R6, record whether the culprit commit was correct, whether the hunk was correct, whether the fix verified, victim runs used, cost, wall time. Ground truth is stored in `bench/ground_truth.json` in the Culprit repo (never in the victim repo). Victim history branches use neutral names (`hist/a`…`hist/f`); the scenario mapping lives only in the Culprit repo.

## 11. Failure handling and recovery

| Failure | Detection | Recovery | Shown in demo? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commit won't install/import | Non-zero exit / import error in worktree | Mark SKIP, test neighbours | **Yes** |
| Noisy result (e.g. 3/5) | Wilson interval straddles threshold | Resample up to cap; flag `low_confidence` | **Yes** |
| Process killed | Ledger has incomplete run | `culprit resume <run_id>` skips completed steps | Yes (short) |
| LLM/API rate limit or 5xx | Exception from SDK | Exponential backoff, then mark step retryable | Trace only |
| Budget cap hit | Ledger cost ≥ cap | Stop, report best current range + what remains | Trace only |
| Fixer patch fails verification | Verifier fails | Retry once with failure evidence, then fall back to verified hunk revert | If it happens |
| Entire context unavailable | CLI error / empty output | Use commit message + diff; report states "intent unavailable" | No |
| No significant regression | good/bad CIs overlap | Exit cleanly with explanation | No |

## 12. Data model (SQLite ledger)

- `runs(run_id, repo, good_ref, bad_ref, suite_hash, config_json, status, started_at, finished_at, total_cost_usd, culprit_sha, confidence)`
- `steps(step_id, run_id, kind[baseline|bisect|resample|localise|fix|verify], commit_sha, status, decision, wilson_low, wilson_high, n, passes, cost_usd, latency_ms_p50, started_at, finished_at, error)`
- `task_runs(id, step_id, task_id, repetition, passed, cost_usd, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, neatlogs_trace_id)`
- `llm_calls(id, run_id, step_id, purpose, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_usd, neatlogs_trace_id)`
- `artifacts(id, run_id, kind[intent|diff|patch|report], path_or_text)`

Every write is idempotent by `(run_id, step kind, commit_sha, task_id, repetition)` so resume never double-counts.

## 13. CLI

```bash
culprit run --repo ../refunddesk --good <ref> --bad <ref> --suite evals/ \
            [--k 3] [--budget-usd 3.00] [--heldout evals/heldout/] [--no-fix]
culprit resume <run_id>
culprit report <run_id> [--html out/report.html]
culprit bench --scenarios bench/scenarios.yaml [--tag v1|v2]
culprit export-costs [--format csv] > costs.csv     # input for cfo.ai
```

**Report contents:** verdict + confidence · bisect timeline (commit, decision, Wilson interval, n, cost, latency) · skipped commits · culprit diff with responsible hunk highlighted · Entire intent + checkpoint link/ID · links to failing neatlogs traces · proposed patch · verification table (good / bad / bad+fix: quality CI, latency, cost) · total cost and victim runs.

## 14. Required tools

### 14.1 neatlogs
- **Tracing:** every victim task run is a trace tagged `commit_sha`, `task_id`, `repetition`, `run_id`. Culprit's own LLM calls are traced separately.
- **Readback:** Task Selector and Localiser pull failing traces via the neatlogs CLI/Public API.
- **Detections:** regex rule on tool results containing `"status": "failed"` followed by `issue_refund`; condition rules such as `cost_usd > <cap>` for runaway runs.
- **Investigate:** used on Culprit **v1** benchmark runs to find why it misidentified or wasted runs.
- **Experiments (prompt versions):** Culprit's Localiser/Task Selector prompts versioned; v1 → v2 promoted by label.
- **Before/after:** `culprit bench --tag v1` and `--tag v2` on the same 6 scenarios. Metrics: culprit accuracy (x/6), hunk accuracy, fix verified (x/6), victim runs per bisect, cost per bisect, wall time. **Numbers are whatever the runs produce; nothing is estimated or rounded in our favour.**

**Instrumentation plan (apply at 12:30, from docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python):**
- Install `pip install -U "neatlogs[anthropic]"` (Python ≥ 3.10, < 3.14). Key from `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` in `.env` (gitignored), never hardcoded. Default endpoint `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`.
- Two workflow names, one per entry point: `culprit-bisect` (Culprit CLI `run`/`resume`/`bench`) and `refunddesk-support-agent` (each victim task run, launched as a subprocess in a worktree).
- Capture Anthropic calls with **one** mechanism only: `neatlogs.wrap(Anthropic())` (the docs example uses OpenAI; Anthropic auto-detection is stated, not shown), or `instrumentations=["anthropic"]` with `init()` before the import. Never both.
- `@neatlogs.span(kind="WORKFLOW")` on each CLI command and on the victim's task entry point; `kind="TOOL"` on mock tools and on Culprit's git/worktree/eval tools; `kind="AGENT"` on Selector/Localiser/Fixer.
- Per-run metadata via `wrap()` kwargs (`commit_sha`, `task_id`, `repetition`, `run_id`), which become `neatlogs.workflow.<key>`. This is inferred from the docs, so verify in the dashboard.
- Both entry points are one-shot processes, so call `neatlogs.flush()` then `neatlogs.shutdown()` at exit (in `finally`).
- Open: the docs don't show how to read the current trace ID. Ask on Discord or use the CLI/Public API to look traces up by `run_id`/`task_id` metadata.

### 14.2 Entire
- Both repos (`piedpiper-neathacks` = Culprit, `refunddesk` = victim) connected via the Entire GitHub App; `entire enable` in each.
- **Product use:** Culprit reads the culprit commit's session context (`entire checkpoint explain <sha>`) to recover intent.
- **Build use:** every meaningful commit of Culprit is checkpointed; the checkpoint for the v1 → v2 fix is the headline evidence (Sessions → Changes).
- **Trails** (if access granted): the v1 → v2 fix done as a Trail. **Graph** optional.
- Submission includes checkpoint link `https://entire.io/gh/OWNER/REPO/commit/FULL_SHA` and checkpoint ID.

### 14.3 cfo.ai
- **Input:** `culprit export-costs` → Google Sheet (cfo.ai lists Google Sheets as a data connection; fall back to manual upload/entry if the import doesn't work).
- **Measured actuals:** cost per victim run, victim runs per bisect, Culprit LLM cost per bisect, wall time.
- **Pricing scenarios to model** (hypotheses, not facts):
  - **A. Flat SaaS:** $49 / $199 per repo/month with a bisect quota.
  - **B. Customer's own model key + platform fee** (recommended hypothesis): customer pays victim-run LLM cost; we charge a platform fee.
  - **C. Metered:** platform fee + per-bisect charge.
- **Questions for Ari:** gross margin per customer under A vs B at 10/50/200 bisects/month · break-even repos with 2 founders · runway under base/upside/downside acquisition · stress test with a 10× more expensive victim agent.
- **Deliverable:** exported business plan (pricing, costs, revenue, runway) in `/business/` and linked from the README.

"""Run configuration. Every field is recorded in the ledger with the run (PRD §8.2)."""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

PROJECT_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
STATE_DIR = PROJECT_ROOT / ".culprit"
WORKTREE_DIR = STATE_DIR / "worktrees"
DEFAULT_DB = STATE_DIR / "ledger.sqlite"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    repo: str
    good_ref: str
    bad_ref: str
    suite: str = "evals"
    k: int = 3
    z: float = 1.96
    budget_usd: float = 3.00
    discriminating_size: int = 8
    install_timeout_s: int = 600
    task_timeout_s: int = 300
    eval_module: str = "refunddesk.eval"
    task_ids: tuple[str, ...] = field(default_factory=tuple)

    def to_json(self) -> str:
        return json.dumps(asdict(self), sort_keys=True)

    @classmethod
    def from_json(cls, text: str) -> Config:
        data = json.loads(text)
        data["task_ids"] = tuple(data.get("task_ids", ()))
        return cls(**data)
